newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - East Europe's chosen few face more sweat to join EU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - East Europe's chosen few face more sweat to join EU.

text.p: The invitation for five leading East European reforming countries to join the European Union is as much a performance bonus as a challenge to speed up bridging the gap separating them from the rich West, analysts say.

Since communism collapsed at the start of the 1990s, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Poland and Slovenia have made giant leaps in transforming their centrally planned societies into western-style market economies. They established functioning democratic systems and focused foreign policy on joining Western security and economic structures.

Rewarding this progress, the European Commission this month recommended that the 15-nation European Union start membership talks with them in early 1998, saying they may become members in four to six years' time.
Yet there is no doubt that the front-runners among the 10 applicants from central and eastern Europe in the race to join the EU face an uphill struggle.

Although they could increase the EU's population by about 17 percent to more than 430 million people, the five have a combined gross domestic product equal to only 6.1 percent of the Union. Their total GDP of 391 billion ecu ($422.1 billion) fails to match that of the Netherlands and Portugal combined.
GDP per capita is much lower, between 23 percent of EU average in Estonia and 59 percent in Slovenia.

None of the front-runners is guaranteed membership, and they must press ahead with economic reform, not least if they are to get in a sufficiently good shape to also enter the bloc's planned single currency later on.

"I would still say that the obstacles are pretty terrific," said economist Stuart Parkinson at investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London. "There are still big issues out there in terms of what they need to do."

Economists said further efforts were needed on several key structural issues, ranging from the reform of costly pension systems and rigid wages to bank privatisation, the restructuring of state-owned enterprises and the deregulation of utilities.

Infrastructure, such as telecommunications and roads, must be expanded rapidly to cope with the anticipated increase in trade. Over-dependence on agriculture is also problematic and the issue is complicated by EU's internal problems with reforming farming policies.
"They have made massive strides but further progress is still necessary," said Wike Groenenberg, senior European economist at Salomon Brothers in London.

This was also highlighted by the European Commission's enlargement document published on July 16, which praised the 10 EU applicants for what they had done so far but made no secret of the fact it felt that more action was necessary.
"In general, structural reform still has a long way to go, particularly as regards the banking and financial systems, and as regards social security," it said.
"I think that our judgement is that there is a lot of ground still to be covered in terms of structural reform," said one Commission official.
NO EU APPLICANT FULLY MEETS CONDITIONS

None of the applicants fully meets the conditions for membership set down by EU leaders in 1993, which centred on achieving a functioning market economy that would be able to stand competition and market forces in the EU.

The commission and analysts agree that Hungary and Poland are closest to satisfying the conditions and the Czech Republic and Slovenia are not far behind. Estonia, the only Baltic state among the chosen few, has furthest to go as its economy seems far from ready to face real-world competitive pressures.

European Commission President Jacques Santer says that even though negotiations over this latest and most ambitious expansion will be difficult, the first countries from beyond the former Iron Curtain could join between 2001 and 2003.
"That is optimistic," said Susanne Hallergard, emerging market economist at investment bank ING Barings in London. "We are looking at a time schedule of at least five years of talks."
She said this would have to do as much with the internal differences in the EU as with the huge adjustment still to be made by the applicants.
"The EU itself is torn on this issue," she said, adding that were it really committed and united on enlargement, the expansion could indeed take place around 2001.
Before enlargement the EU must agree to reform costly agriculture and regional support policies and reach a compromise decision on power and influence in its decision-making institutions.
"The absolutely largest problems are here with us," said Sten Luthman, deputy director at the Stockholm Institute of Transition Economics and East European Economies (SITE).
APPLICANTS' PROGRESS MAY BE UNDERESTIMATED
Hallergard and others stressed the impressive results achieved so far by the five countries.

"They have been able to abandon the planned economy and adopt a fully-fledged, proper, irreversible market economy," Hallergard said. "That is a huge achievement, and underestimated, I think, by everybody."
The private sector is expanding, although the pace of growth differs among the applicants, and at least two of them took steps to overhaul their communist-era social security systems.

Only this month, Hungary's parliament approved a drastic reform of the pension system, and Poland earlier this year took steps to switch from the current hugely expensive pay-as-you-go social security grid.
"This is one of the key questions," said Luthman. He noted that in Poland, for example, pension costs amounted to about 15 percent of gross domestic product. "They can't afford that."

The EU front-runners are also making progress in reducing their budget deficits, crucial if they are ever to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU), due to start in 1999 with the EU countries which meet tough economic conditions.
"Budget deficits and debt are generally not a problem in these countries," said Groenenberg.

From a formal point of view, some East Europeans have public finances in better order than EU heavyweights Germany and France, still struggling to squeeze down their deficits within the required Maastricht treaty limit of three percent of total output.

For example, Estonia's budget is required by law to be in balance, Hungary's deficit fell to 3.2 percent of GDP last year from 6.7 percent in 1995 and Poland plans a shortfall of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product this year.

Hallergard said all five could meet the Maastricht convergence criteria by 2003, with the exception of the currency stability requirement under which a country must have been a member of the EU's exchange rate mechanism for two years.
"So macro-economically they gain magnificently," she said.
Analysts point out, however, that on the enterprise level the gap in efficiency and technological development is still huge.

They also say that the budget deficits of even below three percent are a threat to stability because of the relatively shallow debt markets in these countries and the threat of becoming over-exposed to external borrowing.
There are problems with inflation -- slowing, yet much higher than among EU members -- and with current account deficits, a key reason behind recent pressure on the Czech and Polish currencies.
It was not a surprise therefore that the EU executive made clear that the applicants would probably not be able to join monetary union at the same time as they become members of the EU.

"With respect to the aim of economic and monetary union, it is unlikely that the applicants will be able to join the euro area immediately upon accession," it said in the "Agenda 2000" document, a blueprint for the EU in the 21st century.
However, new members are expected to participate in the EU's exchange rate mechanism, which currently allows fluctuations of 15 percent up or down, and avoid excessive exchange rate changes, it said.
